subtype: Approach: uses trial and error for a small new puzzle [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Indu. Tushar lives next door, and yesterday Tushar found a board game in a box with no rule sheet. Nobody in that house knew how to play it. I expected Tushar to give up, but Tushar just started moving the pieces.
"If I move this one, does it stop?" Tushar said. "Oh, it can't go there. Okay, not that way." Then a card: "Ha, this one sends me back." Every time something went wrong there was a laugh and another try.
I don't know if there was a plan. It looked like working it out as the game went along, and it looked like fun.

qa.q: Where did Tushar find the board game?
qa.a: Tushar found it in a box with no rule sheet.

qa.q: What might Tushar have been feeling while trying the moves?
qa.a: Tushar seemed curious and cheerful, laughing at each mistake, though Indu cannot be sure what Tushar was thinking.

qa.q: What could Tushar do if the game got too confusing to work out?
qa.a: Tushar could ask an older person or look for the rules, since trial and error suits a small puzzle but a stuck game may need help.

qa.q: How does Indu see Tushar's way of learning the game?
qa.a: Indu expected Tushar to give up, but saw a person working it out and having fun, so was a bit surprised.

grounding: A boy facing a new board game with no rules just tries moves and sees what happens, since mistakes cost nothing.

passage:
Saturday: At his friend Suraj's house, Amandeep found an old board game with no rule sheet: wooden pegs, a board of holes and coloured tiles. Suraj shrugged. "Nobody knows how it works."

Sunday: Amandeep came back. "Let's just try moves and see what happens. If it's wrong, who cares? It's only a game." He moved a peg two holes. Nothing. He jumped it over a tile. Suraj gasped. "Maybe that captures it!"

The next Saturday: The boys had invented a full set of rules through trying. Jumping captured tiles, and corners were safe. They'd played eleven rounds. "I think we made it better than the real one," Amandeep said, grinning.

qa.q: How many rounds had the boys played by the next Saturday?
Why was Amandeep happy to just try moves?
qa.a: He felt relaxed and curious, because mistakes cost nothing and playing was the fun part.

qa.q: When would trial and error not be the best approach?
qa.a: When mistakes are costly or unsafe, like with electricity or money, asking an adult or reading instructions is better.

qa.q: How does Suraj see the game by the end?
qa.a: Suraj seems excited and proud, having helped invent rules for a game nobody understood.

grounding: A boy facing a new board game with no rules just tries moves, since mistakes cost nothing and playing is the point.

passage: Aadhya, you want the rules for everything! When I was a boy of ten, in our village near Thrissur, my uncle brought a game from the city: a board with marbles and holes, and the rule paper was lost on the bus. My cousins wanted to wait till someone could explain it. But I thought, "What's the worst that can happen? We lose a game of marbles." So I just started moving them. Jump here, slide there. Some moves were silly and we laughed. Some worked. By evening, we had our own rules and played till dark. Your Joseph Appachan still thinks that was the best game of that holiday. Some things, you just try. Mistakes cost nothing there.

qa.q: Where did young Joseph's uncle bring the game from?
How did young Joseph feel about the missing rules?
qa.a: Young Joseph felt curious and unbothered, thinking the worst that could happen was losing a game of marbles.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the day fun, and why?
qa.a: Joseph deciding to just try moves; it was low-risk and turned the lost rules into a chance to invent their own.

qa.q: How might the cousins have felt when Joseph started moving marbles?
qa.a: They might have been unsure at first, then enjoyed laughing at silly moves and making their own rules.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a boy, trying moves in a board game with no rules, since mistakes cost nothing and playing was the point.
